title: Phillies revamp bullpen, adding Brooks Raley, Caleb Kilian in deadline-day trades
content:
The Athletic has live coverage of the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline.

The Philadelphia Phillies revamped their bullpen via two trades made in quick succession Monday morning, acquiring lefty Brooks Raley from the New York Mets and righty Caleb Kilian from the San Francisco Giants, the latter part of a four-player deal highlighted by Luis Arraez.

Philadelphia’s bullpen has run on fumes in recent weeks, blowing three saves during last week’s road trip to Miami and Baltimore. In July, Phillies relievers produced a 6.13 ERA — second-worst in MLB — and walked 11.5 percent of batters faced — also second-worst in the majors. The bridge to closer Jhoan Duran has consistently been shaky, worsened by Brad Keller’s season-ending ulnar collateral ligament surgery and Orion Kerkering’s recent command struggles.

The left-handed relief situation has been one of the bullpen’s biggest flaws. José Alvarado has had a shaky year, leading the majors in BABIP (batting average on balls in play, .382). Tanner Banks did not live up to his strong 2025 before hitting the injured list with a left forearm strain three weeks ago; he is expected to return later in the season. Kyle Backhus, acquired from the Arizona Diamondbacks in the offseason, has been shaky at times. They are part of a group that has produced a 5.35 ERA in 131 1/3 innings — second-worst among left-handed relievers in the majors.

Bringing in Raley, a proven high-leverage option, should immediately stabilize the situation. Despite his age, the 38-year-old has demonstrated consistency since returning from Tommy John surgery last July. Last season, Raley posted a 2.45 ERA in 30 games (25 2/3 innings). Raley’s numbers remain strong in 2026, even if his command hasn’t looked as sharp at times. He has worked back-to-back days a handful of times this season, though the Mets often followed those occasions with a few days of rest.

Raley has pitched in a range of situations for the struggling Mets, effectively handling high-leverage moments. He is tough on lefties (.186 batting average against) and righties (.216 BAA). For his career, Raley has held left-handed batters to a sub-.600 OPS. Right-handed batters have fared better against him this season compared to the last couple of years, but he generally holds his own against them. Raley throws his sweeper, cutter and sinker to both right-handed and left-handed batters. He could immediately become the bridge to Duran as a reliable option to get the Phillies to their closer.

Raley, who will be a free agent this winter, is owed $1.4 million after Aug. 3. He has not pitched in the postseason since 2022 when he was with the Tampa Bay Rays.

Kilian, 29, is a lesser-known name, but an enticing bullpen addition for the Phillies. He had eight career games in the majors before this season and spent an injury-riddled 2025 in the minors. But he is throwing harder than ever, averaging 97 mph with a fastball that has held opponents to a .296 slugging percentage. He has a 27 percent strikeout rate with a few too many walks, but he fits in the middle of the Phillies’ bullpen. He has five years of club control remaining.

The additions of Kilian and Raley should lessen the Phillies’ reliance on younger bullpen arms like Chase Shugart, Backhus and Seth Johnson; it would be unsurprising if at least two of those pitchers were sent to Triple-A Lehigh Valley in the wake of Monday’s acquisitions. Johnson, who will be out of options in 2027, could be traded if the Phillies decide to move on from him.

The Phillies cultivated strong bullpen depth in the offseason, but so much went wrong this year: poor seasons from their lefties, depth options not panning out, a major injury to Keller. After an extremely shaky July, Kilian and Raley should immediately improve the stability of the bullpen.
